title: 5  Matrix Operations

5.1 Matrix Operations
This module covers the essential matrix operations required for econometrics. We begin with basic matrix creation and arithmetic, progressing to more complex operations like inversion and formal multiplication. Understanding these operations is critical as they form the backbone of the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimator, which we will derive and implement both manually and using built-in R functions.

title: 5  Matrix Operations
text:
5.3 Matrix Addition
In this example, we demonstrate how to add matrices.
We return to the two \((2 \times 2)\) matrices in the previous example and add the matrices together.
\[ \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8
\end{bmatrix} +
\begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\ 15 & 12
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
(2 + 5) & (6 + 2) \\
(4 + 15) & (8 + 12)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
7 & 8 \\
19 & 20
\end{bmatrix}\]
When we add \(m_1\) and \(m_2\), we are adding the values in the same position in each matrix.
For example, for \(m_1\), the value in the first row, first column is equal to 2.
For \(m_2\), the value in the first row, first column is equal to 5.
Adding \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) yields a value of 7 in the first row, first column of the resulting matrix.
The order for matrix addition does not matter, that is, \(m_1 + m_2 = m_2 + m_1\).

5.4 Matrix Subtraction
Using a similar process, we can subtract one matrix from another. While order does not matter for addition, order does matter for subtraction.
If we subtract \(m_2\) from \(m_1\), that is \(m_1 - m_2\), then, we are subtracting the value of each element in \(m_2\) from the corresponding element in \(m_1\).
\[ \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8
\end{bmatrix} -
\begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\ 15 & 12
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
(2 - 5) & (6 - 2) \\
(4 - 15) & (8 - 12)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
-3 & 4 \\
-11 & -4
\end{bmatrix}\]
The value in the first row, first column of \(m_1\) is equal to 5. When we subtract \(m_2\) from \(m_1\), we would subtract 2 (first row, first column of \(m_2\)) from 5 (first row, first column of \(m_1\)), that is, the resulting value is equal to \(2-5 = -3\).
On the other hand, if we subtract \(m_1\) from \(m_2\), then the same position yields \(5-2 = 3\).
\[ \begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\ 15 & 12
\end{bmatrix} -
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8
\end{bmatrix} -
=
\begin{bmatrix}
(5 - 2) & (2 - 6) \\
(15 - 4) & (12 - 8)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
3 & -4 \\
11 & 4
\end{bmatrix}\]

5.5 Hadamard Product
Element-by-element matrix multiplication is straightforward but is not typically used in this class. Element-by-element matrix multiplication is known as the Hadamard Product.
The order of multiplication does not matter, however, the two matrices must have identical dimensions.
Returning to the two matrices, \(m_1\) and \(m_2\), we can conduct element-by-element multiplication by multiplying each element by its corresponding element in the other matrix.
\[
m1 \times m2 =
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\
4 & 8
\end{bmatrix} \times
\begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\
15 & 12
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
(2 \times 5) & (6 \times 2) \\
(4 \times 15) & (8 \times 12)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
10 & 12 \\
60 & 96
\end{bmatrix}
\]

title: 5  Matrix Operations
text:
5.6 Matrix Multiplication
If A is a \((m \times n)\) matrix and B is a \((n \times p)\) matrix, then we can form the matrix product C by AB, if and only if the two matrices are compatible.
The first step is to ensure the matrices are compatible, that is, the inner dimensions of the matrices must match. In this case, the columns in A are equal to the rows in B, so the matrices are compatible.
The resulting matrix will have the dimensions of the ‘outer’ numbers. If we examine this from a dimensional perspective then:
\[
A \times B = (m \times n) \times (n \times p) = (m \times p)
\]
For example, assume that A is \((5 \times 5)\) and B is \((5 \times 8)\). We can form the matrix product AB since the as the number of columns in A is equal to the number of rows in B.

We cannot, however, form the matrix product BA since the number of columns in B is not equal to the number of rows in A.
In general, the only time we are assured that we can multiply AB and BA is when A and B are square matrices with the same dimensions.
Recall that we have previously defined two matrices as:
\[
m_1 = \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\
4 & 8
\end{bmatrix}\]
\[m_2 = \begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\
15 & 12
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Step 1: Top-Left element: Take the first row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the first column of \(m_2\).
\[
(2 \times 5) + (6 \times 15) = 10 + 90 = 100
\]
Step 2: Top-Right Element: Take the first row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the second column of \(m_2\).
\[
(2 \times 2) + (6 \times 12) = 4 + 72 = 76
\]
Step 3: Bottom-Left element: Take the second row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the first column of \(m_2\).
\[
(4 \times 5) + (8 \times 15) = 20 + 120 = 140
\]
Step 4: Bottom-right element: Take the second row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the second column of \(m_2\).
\[
(4 \times 2) + (8 \times 12) = 8 + 96 = 104
\]
When we multiply \(m_1\) by \(m_2\) we obtain a new matrix that is the matrix product or
\[
m_1m_2 = \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\
4 & 8
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\
15 & 12
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
(2 \times 5) + (6 \times 15) & (2 \times 2) + (6 \times 12) \\
(4 \times 5) + (8 \times 15) & (4 \times 2) + (8 \times 12)
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
100 & 76 \\
140 & 104
\end{bmatrix}
\]
To illustrate the point that, in general, matrix multiplication depends on the order of the matrices, we can calculate the product of \(m_2 m_1\).
Step 1: Top-Left element: Take the first row of \(m_2\) and multiply it by the first column of \(m_1\).
\[ (5 \times 2) + (2 \times 4) = 10 + 8 = 18 \]
Step 2: Top-Right Element: Take the first row of \(m_2\) and multiply it by the second column of \(m_1\).
\[ (5 \times 6) + (2 \times 8) = 30 + 16 = 46 \]
Step 3: Bottom-Left element: Take the second row of \(m_2\) and multiply it by the first column of \(m_1\).
\[ (15 \times 2) + (12 \times 4) = 30 + 48 = 78 \]
Step 4: Bottom-right element: Take the second row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the second column of \(m_2\).
\[ (15 \times 6) + (12 \times 8) = 186 \]
When we multiply \(m_1\) by \(m_2\) we obtain a new matrix that is the matrix product or
\[ m_2 m_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 15 & 12  \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8  \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} (5 \times 2) + (2 \times 4) & (5 \times 6) + (2 \times 8) \\ (15 \times 2) + (12 \times 4) & (15 \times 6) + (12 \times 8) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 18 & 46 \\ 78 & 186 \end{bmatrix} \]
This illustrates the point: matrix multiplication is non-communicative. Comparability and order of operations matter. Change the order, obtain a different result.

title: 5  Matrix Operations
text:
5.10 Matrix Inversion
To understand the inverse of a matrix, let’s start with an example where have an equation and we want to solve for the unknown value of \(x\).
\[
5x = 10
\]
We can divide both sides by the reciprocal of 5 to solve for \(x\). \[
\frac{1}{5} \times 5x = 10 \times \frac{1}{5}
\]In other words, if we multiply 5 by it’s inverse, we obtain
\[
5 \times \frac{1}{5} = 1
\]
When we multiply a matrix by its inverse, we obtain the identify matrix (I) which is the matrix equivalent of the number 1 where the identify matrix has 1’s along the diagonal and 0’s off the diagonal or:
\[
A A^{-1} = I =
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & \ldots & 0 \\
0 & 1 & \dots & 0 \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & \ldots & \dots & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Not every matrix, however, has an inverse. A matrix must meet two criteria to have an inverse:

The matrix must be square, that is, the number of rows and columns are equal
The determinant cannot be zero.

Define a \((2 \times 2)\) matrix as:
\[X = \begin{bmatrix}
A & B \\
C & D
\end{bmatrix}\]
The inverse of the \(X\) matrix is denoted as \(X^{-1}\) and is equal to:
\[X^{-1} = \frac{1}{AD - BC} \begin{bmatrix}
D & -B \\
-C & A
\end{bmatrix}\]
We should note that \((AD - BC)\) is the determinant.
Now define \(X\) as:
\[X = \begin{bmatrix}
4 & 8 \\
2 & 6
\end{bmatrix}\]
The inverse of \(X\) or \(X^{-1}\) is equal to:
\[X^{-1} = \frac{1}{(4*6) - (8*2)} \begin{bmatrix}
6 & -8\\
-2 & 4
\end{bmatrix}\]
\[X^{-1} = \frac{1}{8} \begin{bmatrix}
6 & -8\\
-2 & 4
\end{bmatrix}\]
\[X^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}
3/4 & -1\\
-1/4 & 1/2
\end{bmatrix}\]
And if we multiply \(X\) by \(X^{-1}\), we would obtain:
\[X X^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}
4 & 8 \\
2 & 6
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
3/4 & -1\\
-1/4 & 1/2
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
(4*3/4 + -1/4*8) & (4*-1 + 8*1/2) \\
(2*3/4 + 6*-1/4) & (2*-1 + 6*1/2)
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 \\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}=
I\]

title: 6  Linear Regression Models
text:
6.1 Introduction
A linear regression model provides a methodology for examining how the variation in one or more variables may cause variation in a variable of interest.
The variable of interest is the dependent variable and is denoted as \(y\).
The variables that may cause variation in the dependent variable are called the independent variables and are denoted as X.
We hypothesize that the dependent variable is a function of the independent variables or
\[
y = f(X)
\]
A linear regression model assumes the relationship between the dependent variable and independent variables can be models as a linear relationship.
The population regression function can be expressed as:
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_k x_k + \epsilon
\]
Where \(\beta_0\) represents the intercept, that is, the value of \(y\) when the independent variables are 0.
Where \(\beta_1\) through \(\beta_k\) represent the coefficients on the independent variables, that is, the coefficients measure the responsiveness of the dependent variable to a one-unit change in the independent variables.
Where \(\epsilon\) represents the disturbance term or ‘noise’ in our model, that is, the variation in the dependent variable that is not explained by the independent variables.
A linear regression uses data to estimate the coefficients for the independent variables. Why do we need to estimate the coefficients? We do not observe the true values for the coefficients, that is, we do not observe the population parameters in the model.
We use data and linear regression to construct estimates of the population coefficients. If the coefficients are statistically significant, then we interpret the coefficients as representative of the population coefficients.
Unlike physics, it is difficult to replicate experiments in economics. We cannot, for example, restart countries at 1950 to obtain new data. Uncertainty arises from human behavior, measurement error, and a host of other issues.

title: 6  Linear Regression Models
text:
6.2 Useful Notation
A scalar variable is a \((1 \times 1)\) matrix. If \(z = 5\), then \(z\) is a scalar variable.
A column vector is a \((n \times 1)\) matrix, consisting of a single column of \(n\) elements. In most textbooks and linear algebra, the default vector is a column vector.
Assume that our dependent variable, \(y\), has five observations. The dependent variable is a column vector that has 5 rows and 1 column, that is, \(y \sim (5 \times 1)\) or:
\[\boldsymbol{y} = \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ y_3 \\ y_4 \\ y_5 \end{bmatrix}\]
A row vector is a \((1 \times k)\) matrix, consisting of a single row of \(k\) elements.
Assumes that we have data on a single individual’s age, height, weight, income, and education. The row vector containing this data might look like:
\[\begin{bmatrix}
32 \, years & 72 \, inches & 190 \, pounds & 75,000 & 18 \, years
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Note that we can transform a column vector into a row vector using the transpose operation. Returning to our column vector \(y\), we can take the transpose of \(y\) to obtain a \(1 \times 5\) row vector or:
\[y^T =\begin{bmatrix}
y_1 & y_2 & y_3 & y_4 & y_5
\end{bmatrix}
\]
A matrix, \(\boldsymbol{X}\) with dimensions \((n \times K)\) is
\[\boldsymbol{X} = \begin{bmatrix}
x_{11} & x_{12} & \dots & x_{1K} \\
x_{21} & x_{22} & \dots & x_{2K} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \dots & x_{nK}
\end{bmatrix}\]
The first subscript of an element gives the row position while the second subscript of the element gives the column position.

title: 6  Linear Regression Models
text:
6.3 Expectations
The expected value of a random variable is the arithmetic mean of the variable, that is,
\[E[X] = \mu_x\]
In the discrete case, the expected value of a random variable \(X\) is found by multiplying each \(x\) by its probability and then summing over the random variable or:
\[E[X] = \sum x \, p(x) = \mu_x\]
In the continuous case, the expectation is defined by:
\[E[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, f(x) \, dx = \mu_x\]
We can show that the variance of \(X\) is equal to
\[\sigma_X^2 = E[(X-\mu)^2] = E(X^2) - (E[X])^2\]
\[\sigma_X^2 = E\bigg[(X-\mu)^2 \bigg] = E \bigg[(X-\mu) \, (X-\mu) \bigg]\] \[\sigma_X^2 = E\bigg[(X^2 - \mu\,X - X \mu + \mu^2) \bigg]\] Since \(\mu\) is a scalar, we know that \(E[\mu X] = \mu E[X]\)
\[\sigma_X^2 = E\bigg[(X^2 - 2\mu X + \mu^2) \bigg]\] \[\sigma_X^2 = E[X^2] - 2 \mu E[X] + \mu^2\] \[\sigma_X^2 = E[X^2] - 2 \mu^2 + \mu^2 = E[X^2] - \mu^2 = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2\]

title: 6  Linear Regression Models
text:
6.4 Linearity
If the assumptions of the linear regression model hold, then the linear regression model will produce useful estimates of the unknown population parameters.
Let the column vector \(\boldsymbol{x}_k\) be the \(n\) observations on variable \(x_k\) where \(k = 1, 2, ..., K\) in a random sample of \(n\) observations.
Assemble the \(k\) column vectors over \(n\) observations to obtain an \((n \times K)\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{X}\).
The first column of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) or \(\boldsymbol{x}_1\) is a column of 1s so that \(\beta_1\) the constant term in the linear regression model.
Let \(\boldsymbol{y}\) be \((n \times 1)\) column vector containing the \(n\) observations \(y_1, y_2, ..., y_n\).
Let \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) be \((n \times 1)\) column vector containing the \(n\) observations \(\epsilon_1, \epsilon_2, ..., \epsilon_n\).
Let \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) be the \((k \times 1)\) parameter vector containing the \(k\) population parameters \(\beta_1, \beta_2, ..., \beta_k\).
The linear regression model can be written as:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_n
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & x_{12} &\dots & x_{1K} \\
1 & x_{22} &\dots & x_{2K} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
1 & x_{n2} &\dots & x_{nK}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\beta_1 \\ \beta_2 \\ \vdots \\ \beta_K
\end{bmatrix} +
\begin{bmatrix}
\epsilon_1 \\ \epsilon_2 \\ \vdots \\ \epsilon_n
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The linear regression model can also be written as:
\[\boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{X \beta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}\]

title: 6  Linear Regression Models
text:
6.5 Full Rank
The assumption of full rank or no perfect colinearity is that there are no exact linear relationships among the independent variables.
The assumption of full rank implies that \(\boldsymbol{X}\) has full column rank, that is, there is no \(\boldsymbol{x}_k\) that is an exact linear combination of one or more other \(\boldsymbol{x}_k\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\).
The assumption of full rank also implies that are at least \(K\) observations in \(\boldsymbol{X}\).
The assumptions of full column rank and \(K\) observations are known as the identification condition.
If a model is non-identifiable, the true population parameters cannot be ascertained.
Assume X is \((5 x 5)\) can be expressed as:
\[\boldsymbol{X} = \begin{bmatrix}
x_{11} & x_{12} & x_{13} & x_{14} & x_{15} \\
x_{21} & x_{22} & x_{23} & x_{24} & x_{25} \\
x_{31} & x_{32} & x_{33} & x_{34} & x_{35} \\
x_{41} & x_{42} & x_{43} & x_{44} & x_{45} \\
x_{51} & x_{52} & x_{53} & x_{54} & x_{55} \end{bmatrix}\]
What would happen if
\[
x_2 = x_3 + x_4
\]
First, \(x_2\) is a perfect linear combination of \(x_3\) and \(x_4\) and, because of this, \(X\) is short rank.
Because \(X\) is short rank, no unique solution exists for the linear regression parameter estimates.
In the code example below, we create two \((4 \times 4)\) matrices.
In the first matrix, the third column is equal to the square of the second column.
\[
x_{3} = x_2^{2}
\]
Even though \(x_3\) is equal to the square of \(x_2\), you cannot create \(x_3\) by multiplying \(x_2\) by a single scalar value, unless \(x_2\) is all 1’s or 0’s. The columns of X are linearly independent and the matrix is full rank.
In the second matrix, the third column is equal to the sum of the first two columns or:
\[
x_3 = x_1 + x_2
\]
In this case, \(x_3\) is a perfect linear combination of \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). The X matrix is short rank.
Let X be a \((n \times K)\) matrix of independent variables. A key element of a linear regression model is:
\[
(X^T X)^{-1}
\]
For this inverse to exist, the determinant must be non-zero.
We can use the det function in R to calculate the determinant of each matrix.
We find that the determinant of the first matrix, \(X_1\), is non-zero, while the determinant of the second matrix, \(X_2\), is equal to zero.
Because the determinant of \(X_2\) is equal to zero, the inverse of \(X_2\) does not exist.
What about
\[
(X_1^T X_1) \\
(X_2^T X_2)
\]
We can use the det function to find that the determinant of \(X_1^T X_1\) is non-zero while the determinant of \(X_2^T X_2\) is equal to zero.
In other words, because \(X_2\) is short rank, \(X_2^T X_2\) is also short rank, and the inverse does not exist.

title: 6  Linear Regression Models
text:
6.6 Zero Conditional Mean
Recall that the linear regression model is written as:
\[\boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{X \beta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}\]
Where the \(\epsilon\) represents the disturbance term in the linear regression model.
The assumption of Zero Conditional Mean is that the expected value of the disturbance in the linear regression model is not a function of the independent variables, that is, the independent variables contain no useful information regarding the prediction of \(\epsilon\).
The assumption of Zero Conditional Mean is
\[
E[\epsilon_i \, | \, \boldsymbol{X}] = 0 \quad \forall \, i
\]
and implies that the mean of each \(\epsilon_i\) conditional on all \(\boldsymbol{x_j}\) is zero. In other words, no independent variable conveys information about the disturbances.
The assumption that there is no information in \(\boldsymbol{X}\) about any \(\epsilon_i\) is the strict exogeneity assumption.
The mean independence of the disturbances implies that the mean of the disturbances is zero or
\[
E[\epsilon] =  E[E[\epsilon_i | \boldsymbol{X}]] = E[0 | X] = 0
\]
Zero Conditional Mean also implies that no disturbance contains information about other disturbances, that is, the disturbances are independent of each other or:
\[
E[\epsilon_i | \epsilon_j] = 0 \quad \forall i \ne j
\]
Zero conditional mean implies that \(cov(\epsilon_i |\boldsymbol{X}) = 0\). This will be important later.

title: 6  Linear Regression Models
text:
6.7 Unbiasedness
The assumptions of linearity, full rank, and zero conditional mean allow us to form the linear regression model and obtain estimates of the population parameters.
The question remains, however, are the estimates representative for the population parameters?
The regression of \(\boldsymbol{y}\) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is the conditional mean or:
\[E[\boldsymbol{y}|\boldsymbol{X}]\]
Assume that linearity, full rank, and zero conditional mean hold and the linear regression model is: \[\boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{X \beta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}\]
\[E[\boldsymbol{y}|\boldsymbol{X}] = E[(\boldsymbol{X \beta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon})|\boldsymbol{X}] = E[(\boldsymbol{X \beta})|\boldsymbol{X}] + E[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}|\boldsymbol{X}] = \boldsymbol{X \beta}\]
If the zero conditional mean assumption does not hold, then
\[E[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}|\boldsymbol{X}] \ne 0\]
\[E[\boldsymbol{y}|\boldsymbol{X}] = \boldsymbol{X \beta} + E[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}|\boldsymbol{X}]\]
As the covariance between \(\epsilon\) and \(\boldsymbol{X}\) increases, that is, as \(\boldsymbol{X}\) contains more information about \(\epsilon\), the linear regression model will not produce ‘reliable’ estimates of the population parameters of interest.
Simply put, if Zero Conditional Mean fails, the linear regression model produces biased estimates of the population parameters.

title: 6  Linear Regression Models
text:
6.8 Homosecdasticity
The variance of the disturbances conditional on the independent variables is constant and the covariance among the disturbances conditional on the independent variables is equal to zero.
The assumption of homoscedasticity is:
\[var[\epsilon_i |\boldsymbol{X}] = \sigma^2 \quad \forall i\]
The assumption of no autocorrelation is
\[cov[\epsilon_i, \epsilon_j | \boldsymbol{X}] = 0 \quad \forall i,j\]
Homoscedasticity implies that the variance of the disturbances is independent of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and constant, that is, the independent variables contain no information about the dispersion of the disturbances.
The assumption of no autocorrelation implies that the covariance of the disturbances, conditional on the independent variables, is equal to zero, that is, no disturbance contains information about any other disturbance.
Together, the assumptions imply that the diagonal of the variance-covariance matrix for the disturbances consists of \(\sigma^2\) and the off-diagonal terms are 0.
Let the variance of the disturbance be \(E[\epsilon \epsilon^T |\boldsymbol{X} ] =\)
\[\begin{bmatrix}
E[\epsilon_1^2|X] & E[\epsilon_1 \epsilon_2|X] & \dots  & E[\epsilon_1 \epsilon_n|X]  \\
E[\epsilon_2 \epsilon_1|X] & E[\epsilon_2^2|X] & \dots  & E[\epsilon_2 \epsilon_n|X]  \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots                                                     \\
E[\epsilon_n \epsilon_1|X] & E[\epsilon_n \epsilon_2|X] & \dots  & E[\epsilon_n^2|X]  
\end{bmatrix}\]
Using the assumptions of homoscedasticity and no autocorrelation yields:
\[\begin{bmatrix}
\sigma^2 & 0 & \ddots & 0  \\
0 & \sigma^2 & \ddots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots                                                     \\
0 & 0 & \ddots & \sigma^2
\end{bmatrix}\]
What does this mean?
\[E[\epsilon \epsilon^T | \boldsymbol{X}] = \sigma^2 \boldsymbol{I}\]
where \(\boldsymbol{I}\) is an \((n \times k)\) identity matrix consisting of 1’s on the diagonal and 0’s off the diagonal.
In other words, the variance-covariance matrix for the disturbances is, under the assumption of homoscedasticity, equal to a constant, \(\sigma^2\) times an identity matrix.

title: 6  Linear Regression Models
text:
6.9 Data Generation
Social scientists cannot, in many circumstances, create and run experiments. If we could, then regressors would be nonrandom. Instead, we often rely on observational data the results from a stochastic process.
We also use dummy variables to capture specific events or characteristics. A constant may be used to capture a starting or ending point of a process. In other words, we may also use non-stochastic data.
In macroeconomics, the date of colonial independence is often used in regressions of Gross Domestic Product on determinants of economic development as a control variable. These regressions mix stochastic (investment, exports, democracy) and non-stochastic (colonial independence, legal system dummy) data.
Assumption 5 is that the regressors may be fixed or random, that is, the matrix of independent variables may contain stochastic (random) and non-stochastic (non-random) variables.

title: 6  Linear Regression Models
text:
6.10 Normal Disturbances
Assumption 3 (Zero Conditional Mean) implies that that the conditional mean of the disturbances is zero
\[
E[\epsilon_i | \boldsymbol{X}] = 0
\]
Assumption 4 implies that the conditional variance of the disturbances is equal to \(\sigma^2 I\) or
\[
E[\epsilon^T \epsilon | \boldsymbol{X}] = E[\epsilon^T \epsilon] = \sigma^2 I
\]
Assumption 6 is that the disturbances are normally distributed or
\[
\epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2I)
\]
This assumption is useful for inference, however, it is also restrictive.
For our purposes, the normality of the disturbances is a useful starting point.

title: 6  Linear Regression Models
text:
6.11 Linear Regression Model
If the assumptions of the linear regression model hold, we can show that the model produces reasonable estimates of the unknown population parameters.
The first three assumptions are:

Linearity
Full Rank
Zero Conditional Mean

If these assumptions hold, the linear regression model will produce unbiased estimates.
The second three assumptions are:

Homoscedasticity
Data generation
Normality of the disturbances

Let the two-variable linear regression model be
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \boldsymbol{x} + \epsilon\]
If the assumptions hold, then \[E[y] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \boldsymbol{x}\]
Different textbooks have different conventions. Sometimes the intercept is \(\beta_0\), sometimes \(\beta_1\). There is no significant impact on derivation.

title: 6  Linear Regression Models
text:
6.12 Violating the Assumptions
In this course, we will focus on violations of the assumptions of the exogeneity of the regressors and homoscedasticity.
If the regressors and the disturbances are independent but the variance of the disturbances is a function of the regressors, then the variance of the disturbances is no longer constant.
If this occurs, the estimates of the standard errors of the parameter estimates are not reliable and we cannot make inferences about the statistical significance of the parameter estimates.
We will show that if one or more regressors are endogenous then the parameter estimates do not, on average equal the population parameters.
We will also show that if one or more regressors are endogenous that the parameter estimates do not converge to the population parameters.
We will need to modify our approach to account for endogeneity, heteroscedasticity, or both.

8.3 Matrix Addition
In this example, we demonstrate how to add matrices.
We return to the two \((2 \times 2)\) matrices in the previous example and add the matrices together.
\[ \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8
\end{bmatrix} +
\begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\ 15 & 12
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
(2 + 5) & (6 + 2) \\
(4 + 15) & (8 + 12)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
7 & 8 \\
19 & 20
\end{bmatrix}\]
When we add \(m_1\) and \(m_2\), we are adding the values in the same position in each matrix.
For example, for \(m_1\), the value in the first row, first column is equal to 2.
For \(m_2\), the value in the first row, first column is equal to 5.
Adding \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) yields a value of 7 in the first row, first column of the resulting matrix.
The order for matrix addition does not matter, that is, \(m_1 + m_2 = m_2 + m_1\).

8.4 Matrix Subtraction
Using a similar process, we can subtract one matrix from another. While order does not matter for addition, order does matter for subtraction.
If we subtract \(m_2\) from \(m_1\), that is \(m_1 - m_2\), then, we are subtracting the value of each element in \(m_2\) from the corresponding element in \(m_1\).
\[ \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8
\end{bmatrix} -
\begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\ 15 & 12
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
(2 - 5) & (6 - 2) \\
(4 - 15) & (8 - 12)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
-3 & 4 \\
-11 & -4
\end{bmatrix}\]
The value in the first row, first column of \(m_1\) is equal to 5. When we subtract \(m_2\) from \(m_1\), we would subtract 2 (first row, first column of \(m_2\)) from 5 (first row, first column of \(m_1\)), that is, the resulting value is equal to \(2-5 = -3\).
On the other hand, if we subtract \(m_1\) from \(m_2\), then the same position yields \(5-2 = 3\).

8.5 Hadamard Product
Element-by-element matrix multiplication is straightforward but is not typically used in this class. Element-by-element matrix multiplication is known as the Hadamard Product.
The order of multiplication does not matter, however, the two matrices must have identical dimensions.
Returning to the two matrices, \(m_1\) and \(m_2\), we can conduct element-by-element multiplication by multiplying each element by its corresponding element in the other matrix.
\[

\begin{bmatrix}

4 & 8
\end{bmatrix} \times
\begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\
15 & 12
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
(2 \times 5) & (6 \times 2) \\
(4 \times 15) & (8 \times 12)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
10 & 12 \\
60 & 96
\end{bmatrix}
\]

title: 8  Matrix Operations
text:
8.6 Matrix Multiplication
If A is a \((m \times n)\) matrix and B is a \((n \times p)\) matrix, then we can form the matrix product C by AB, if and only if the two matrices are compatible.
The first step is to ensure the matrices are compatible, that is, the inner dimensions of the matrices must match. In this case, the columns in A are equal to the rows in B, so the matrices are compatible.
The resulting matrix will have the dimensions of the ‘outer’ numbers. If we examine this from a dimensional perspective then:
\[
A \times B = (m \times n) \times (n \times p) = (m \times p)
\]
For example, assume that A is \((5 \times 5)\) and B is \((5 \times 8)\). We can form the matrix product AB since the as the number of columns in A is equal to the number of rows in B.

We cannot, however, form the matrix product BA since the number of columns in B is not equal to the number of rows in A.
In general, the only time we are assured that we can multiply AB and BA is when A and B are square matrices with the same dimensions.
Recall that we have previously defined two matrices as:
\[
m_1 = \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\
4 & 8
\end{bmatrix}\]
\[m_2 = \begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\
15 & 12
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Step 1: Top-Left element: Take the first row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the first column of \(m_2\).
\[
(2 \times 5) + (6 \times 15) = 10 + 90 = 100
\]
Step 2: Top-Right Element: Take the first row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the second column of \(m_2\).
\[
(2 \times 2) + (6 \times 12) = 4 + 72 = 76
\]
Step 3: Bottom-Left element: Take the second row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the first column of \(m_2\).
\[
(4 \times 5) + (8 \times 15) = 20 + 120 = 140
\]
Step 4: Bottom-right element: Take the second row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the second column of \(m_2\).
\[
(4 \times 2) + (8 \times 12) = 8 + 96 = 104
\]
When we multiply \(m_1\) by \(m_2\) we obtain a new matrix that is the matrix product or
\[
m_1m_2 = \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 6 \\
4 & 8
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
5 & 2 \\
15 & 12
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
(2 \times 5) + (6 \times 15) & (2 \times 2) + (6 \times 12) \\
(4 \times 5) + (8 \times 15) & (4 \times 2) + (8 \times 12)
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
100 & 76 \\
140 & 104
\end{bmatrix}
\]
To illustrate the point that, in general, matrix multiplication depends on the order of the matrices, we can calculate the product of \(m_2 m_1\).
Step 1: Top-Left element: Take the first row of \(m_2\) and multiply it by the first column of \(m_1\).
\[ (5 \times 2) + (2 \times 4) = 10 + 8 = 18 \]
Step 2: Top-Right Element: Take the first row of \(m_2\) and multiply it by the second column of \(m_1\).
\[ (5 \times 6) + (2 \times 8) = 30 + 16 = 46 \]
Step 3: Bottom-Left element: Take the second row of \(m_2\) and multiply it by the first column of \(m_1\).
\[ (15 \times 2) + (12 \times 4) = 30 + 48 = 78 \]
Step 4: Bottom-right element: Take the second row of \(m_1\) and multiply it by the second column of \(m_2\).
\[ (15 \times 6) + (12 \times 8) = 186 \]
When we multiply \(m_1\) by \(m_2\) we obtain a new matrix that is the matrix product or
\[ m_2 m_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 15 & 12  \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8  \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} (5 \times 2) + (2 \times 4) & (5 \times 6) + (2 \times 8) \\ (15 \times 2) + (12 \times 4) & (15 \times 6) + (12 \times 8) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 18 & 46 \\ 78 & 186 \end{bmatrix} \]
This illustrates the point: matrix multiplication is non-communicative. Comparability and order of operations matter. Change the order, obtain a different result.

8.8 Idempotent Matrix
An idempotent matrix is one which, when multiplied by itself, yields itself.
If a matrix \(A\) is idempotent, then \(A \times A = A\).
\[M = \begin{bmatrix}
3 & -6 \\
1 & -2
\end{bmatrix}\]
\[
MM = \begin{bmatrix}
3 & -6 \\
1 & -2
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
3 & -6 \\
1 & -2
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
(3*3)+(1*-6) & (3*1)+(1*-2)\\

3 & -6 \\

8.10 Matrix Inversion
To understand the inverse of a matrix, let’s start with an example where have an equation and we want to solve for the unknown value of \(x\).
\[
5x = 10
\]
We can divide both sides by the reciprocal of 5 to solve for \(x\). \[
\frac{1}{5} \times 5x = 10 \times \frac{1}{5}
\]In other words, if we multiply 5 by it’s inverse, we obtain
\[
5 \times \frac{1}{5} = 1
\]
When we multiply a matrix by its inverse, we obtain the identify matrix (I) which is the matrix equivalent of the number 1 where the identify matrix has 1’s along the diagonal and 0’s off the diagonal or:
\[
A A^{-1} = I =
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & \ldots & 0 \\
0 & 1 & \dots & 0 \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & \ldots & \dots & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Not every matrix, however, has an inverse. A matrix must meet two criteria to have an inverse:

The matrix must be square, that is, the number of rows and columns are equal
The determinant cannot be zero.

Define a \((2 \times 2)\) matrix as:
\[X = \begin{bmatrix}
A & B \\
C & D
\end{bmatrix}\]
The inverse of the \(X\) matrix is denoted as \(X^{-1}\) and is equal to:
\[X^{-1} = \frac{1}{AD - BC} \begin{bmatrix}
D & -B \\
-C & A
\end{bmatrix}\]
We should note that \((AD - BC)\) is the determinant.
Now define \(X\) as:
\[X = \begin{bmatrix}
4 & 8 \\
2 & 6
\end{bmatrix}\]
The inverse of \(X\) or \(X^{-1}\) is equal to:
\[X^{-1} = \frac{1}{(4*6) - (8*2)} \begin{bmatrix}
6 & -8\\
-2 & 4
\end{bmatrix}\]
\[X^{-1} = \frac{1}{8} \begin{bmatrix}
6 & -8\\
-2 & 4
\end{bmatrix}\]
\[X^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}
3/4 & -1\\
-1/4 & 1/2
\end{bmatrix}\]
And if we multiply \(X\) by \(X^{-1}\), we would obtain:
\[X X^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}
4 & 8 \\
2 & 6
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
3/4 & -1\\
-1/4 & 1/2
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
(4*3/4 + -1/4*8) & (4*-1 + 8*1/2) \\
(2*3/4 + 6*-1/4) & (2*-1 + 6*1/2)
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 \\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}=
I\]
In the code below, we create a \((2 \times 2)\) matrix and use the solve function in R to calculate the inverse of the square matrix. We then multiply the matrix by its inverse to obtain the identity matrix.

8.4 Estimating Using LM Function
We can also compare the least squares estimates using matrix algebra with those obtained using the lm function (which uses matrix algebra behind the scenes).
In the example below, we replicate the methodology above to obtain the least squares estimates using matrix algebra. Note that we have changed the number of observations to 10,000.

8.5 Matrix Properties
In this section, we list some common matrix properties which are useful in econometrics.
For much more information, see “The Matrix Cookbook” at http://matrixcookbook.com
Vectors are lowercase letters while capital letters represent matrices.
The transpose operation reverses the order of an operation so that the transpose of a product of two matrices can be expressed as the product of the transposed matrices in reverse order.
\[(AB)^T = B^T A^T\]
Let \(a\) and \(c\) be vectors.
The transpose operator reverses the order of the operation.
The transpose of a transposed vector is the vector.
\[(a^T B c)^T = c^T B^T a\]
\((A + B)\) pre-multiplies \(C\) is equal to the distributed addition of \(AC\) and \(BC\).
\[(A+B)C = AC + BC\]
The transpose of the addition of the vectors \(a\) and \(b\) pre-multiplies \(C\) and the multiplication can be distributed.
\[(a+b)^T C = a^T C + b^T C\]
As noted previously, in almost every case, matrix multiplication is not communicative.
\[AB \ne BA\]
In the code below, we demonstrate each of these properties.

text:
8.6 Common Derivative Properties
The following rules are often quite useful
First, let’s state derivative properties with respect to scalars.
The derivative of \(bx\) with respect to \(x\) is \(b\).
\[\frac{\partial bx}{\partial x} = b \]
The derivative of \(x^2\) with respect to \(x\) is \(2x\).
\[\frac{\partial x^2}{\partial x} = 2x\]
The derivative of \(bx^2\) with respect to \(x\) is \(2bx\).
\[\frac{\partial b x^2}{\partial x} = 2bx\]
We can take these scalar rules and apply them in a similar fashion of vectors and matrices.
\[\frac{\partial x^T B}{\partial x} = B\]
\[\frac{\partial x^T b}{\partial x} = b\]
\[\frac{\partial x^T x}{\partial x} = 2x\] \[\frac{\partial x^T B x}{\partial x} = (B + B^T)x = 2Bx \]

8.11 Projection Matrix
While \(My\) captures the unexplained variation in \(y\), \(Py\) captured the explained variation in \(y\) or:
\[M = I - X(X^T X)^{-1}X^T\]
\[P = X(X^T X)^{-1}X^T\]
The projection matrix \(P\) is symmetric and idempotent.
\(PM\) and \(MP\) are equivalent and equal to zero and \(P\) and \(M\) are orthogonal.
Given the orthogonality, we can partition y into two parts:
\[y = Py + My\] \[y = X(X^T X)^{-1} X^T y + (I-X(X^T X)^{-1}X^T)y\]
Recall that \(b = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y\) and substitute:
\[y = Xb + (I-X(X^T X)^{-1}X^T)y\]
Now multiply \(y\) through the second term:
\[y = X b + (y - X(X^T X)^{-1} X^T y)\]
Substitute again for \(b\)
\[y = X b + (y - X b)\]
Recognize that \(Xb = \hat{y}\)
\[y = Xb + (y - \hat{y})\] \[y = Xb + e\]

8.7 Residual Maker Matrix
\(M\) is a \((n \times n)\) symmetric, idempotent matrix where
\[M = I - X(X^T X)^{-1}X^T\]
\(M\) is the residual maker matrix.
When \(y\) is pre-multiplied by \(M\), it produces the vector of least squares residuals, \(e\).
\[
My = (I - X(X^TX)^{-1} X^T = y - X(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty = y - Xb = e
\]
We also note that \(MX = 0\) because the regression of \(X\) on \(X\) is a ‘perfect fit’ or:
\[
MX = (I - X(X^TX)^{-1} X^T)X = X - X(X^TX)^{-1}X^TX = X - X = 0
\]

In this section, we discuss the motivation behind least squares regression before deriving the least squares estimator. We then examine the small sample properties of the least squares estimator. We explore how the dependent variable can be decomposed into explained and unexplained variation through the use of the residual maker and projection matrices.

9.3 Estimating Coefficients
We can now specify the population coefficients, that is, as we are simulating population data, we can define the values of the population parameters or:
\[
\beta = \begin{bmatrix}{1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \\ 4 \\ 5 \\ 6} \end{bmatrix}
\] Let the disturbance term, \(\epsilon\) be distributed normally with 0 mean and constant variance equal to 1 or:
\[
\epsilon \sim N(0,1)
\] We specify that \(y\) is a linear equation equal to:
\[
y = X \beta + \epsilon
\]
The least squares estimator is defined as:
\[
b = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y
\]
We estimate the least squares coefficients and produce a table of coefficients.
You should note that even though we have population data and know the population parameters, the least squares estimates are not equal to the population parameters.
The stochastic disturbance captures unobserved variation in the dependent variable, that is, we can not fully explain the variation in the dependent variable.

9.4 Estimating Using LM Function
We can also compare the least squares estimates using matrix algebra with those obtained using the lm function (which uses matrix algebra behind the scenes).
In the example below, we replicate the methodology above to obtain the least squares estimates using matrix algebra. Note that we have changed the number of observations to 10,000.
To use the lm function and obtain results comparable to those using matrix algebra, we only need to include the independent variables. This means we must exclude the intercept variable (X1) from the data that will be used by the lm function.
Why?
The lm function, by default, estimates an intercept. If we included the intercept variable (which is a column of 1’s in the X matrix), then our results would not be comparable.
We find that the estimates are the same, regardless if we use matrix algebra or the lm function.

9.5 Matrix Properties
In this section, we list some common matrix properties which are useful in econometrics.
For much more information, see “The Matrix Cookbook” at http://matrixcookbook.com
Vectors are lowercase letters while capital letters represent matrices.
The transpose operation reverses the order of an operation so that the transpose of a product of two matrices can be expressed as the product of the transposed matrices in reverse order.
\[(AB)^T = B^T A^T\]
Let \(a\) and \(c\) be vectors.
The transpose operator reverses the order of the operation.
The transpose of a transposed vector is the vector.
\[(a^T B c)^T = c^T B^T a\]
\((A + B)\) pre-multiplies \(C\) is equal to the distributed addition of \(AC\) and \(BC\).
\[(A+B)C = AC + BC\]
The transpose of the addition of the vectors \(a\) and \(b\) pre-multiplies \(C\) and the multiplication can be distributed.
\[(a+b)^T C = a^T C + b^T C\]
As noted previously, in almost every case, matrix multiplication is not communicative.
\[AB \ne BA\]
In the code below, we demonstrate each of these properties.

text:
9.6 Common Derivative Properties
The following rules are often quite useful
First, let’s state derivative properties with respect to scalars.
The derivative of \(bx\) with respect to \(x\) is \(b\).
\[\frac{\partial bx}{\partial x} = b \]
The derivative of \(x^2\) with respect to \(x\) is \(2x\).
\[\frac{\partial x^2}{\partial x} = 2x\]
The derivative of \(bx^2\) with respect to \(x\) is \(2bx\).
\[\frac{\partial b x^2}{\partial x} = 2bx\]
We can take these scalar rules and apply them in a similar fashion of vectors and matrices.
\[\frac{\partial x^T B}{\partial x} = B\]
\[\frac{\partial x^T b}{\partial x} = b\]
\[\frac{\partial x^T x}{\partial x} = 2x\] \[\frac{\partial x^T B x}{\partial x} = (B + B^T)x = 2Bx \]

9.11 Residual Maker Matrix
The vector of least square residuals is \(\boldsymbol{e} = \boldsymbol{y} - \boldsymbol{X b}\).
Substituting for \(\boldsymbol{b}\) yields:
\[\boldsymbol{e} = \boldsymbol{y} - \boldsymbol{X b}\] \[\boldsymbol{e} = \boldsymbol{y} - \boldsymbol{X (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y}\] \[\boldsymbol{e} = (\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{X (X^T X)^{-1} X^T})\boldsymbol{y}\] \[\boldsymbol{e} = \boldsymbol{M y}\]
\[\boldsymbol{M} = (\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{X (X^T X)^{-1} X^T})\]
M is defined as the residual maker or the annihilator matrix.

9.10 Projection Matrix
We have previously defined our linear regression model as:
\[
\boldsymbol{y = X\beta + \epsilon = Xb + e}
\]
We know that our predicted values are equal to:
\[
\boldsymbol{\hat{y} = Xb = y - e}
\]
We can use this to object the projection matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\) \[\boldsymbol{\hat{y}} = \boldsymbol{Xb}\] \[\boldsymbol{\hat{y}} = \boldsymbol{X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T y}\]
\[\boldsymbol{\hat{y}} = \boldsymbol{X (X^T X)^{-1} X^Ty} = \boldsymbol{P y}\]
\[\boldsymbol{P} = \boldsymbol{X (X^T X)^{-1} X^T}\]
The projection matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\) is symmetric and idempotent.

9.2 Notation
Define a column vector \(\boldsymbol{x_k}\) such that \(\boldsymbol{x_k}\) consists of \(n\) observations.
Let \(k \in \{1, 2, \dots, K\}\) such that \(\boldsymbol{x_1}\) is the first column vector.
Let \(\boldsymbol{x_2}\) be the second column vector, and so on.
Combining the column vectors for \(\boldsymbol{x_k}\) yields a \((n \times K)\) matrix.
The first column of the resulting \(\boldsymbol{X}\) matrix consists of a column of 1’s.
The subscript \(k\) refers to the k-th column of the \(\boldsymbol{X}\) matrix.
The subscript \(i\) refers to the i-th row of the \(\boldsymbol{X}\) matrix.
The linear regression model is equal to:
\[\boldsymbol{y = X \, \beta + \epsilon}\]
\[\begin{bmatrix}
y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_n
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
x_{11} & x_{12} & \dots & x_{1K} \\
x_{21} & x_{22} & \dots & x_{2K} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
x_{n1} & x_{n2} & x_{n3} & x_{nK}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\beta_1 \\
\beta_2 \\
\beta_3 \\
\beta_4
\end{bmatrix} +
\begin{bmatrix}
\epsilon_1 \\
\epsilon_2 \\
\vdots \\
\epsilon_n
\end{bmatrix}\]

title: 9  Deriving Least Squares
text:
9.3 Why Least Squares?
Assume that we wish to estimate the impact of education on workers’ salaries. We specify a linear regression model where salary is a function of education and other explanatory variables or:
\[
salary = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \, education + \beta_3 \, age + \dots + \beta_k x_K + \epsilon
\]
We do not observe the population parameters.
We need an algorithm or rule by which we can develop estimates of the population parameters.
The algorithm or rule is called an estimator.
When we use the estimator with data, we produce estimates of the population parameters.
What is our objective?
We want an algorithm or rule that produces estimates that are “close” to the actual values.
In other words, we want an estimator to produce estimates that are “close” to the actual values of the dependent variable.
We can define our estimates of the population parameters as b.
We can define our predicted values of the dependent variable as \(\hat{y}\).
Our predicted values are equal to:
\[
\hat{y} = Xb = b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + \dots + b_k x_k
\]
And our “mistakes” or “residuals” are defined as:
\[
e = y - \hat{y} = y - Xb
\]
So, what is our objective function?
We could try and minimize the sum of our mistakes or:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n = y_i - \hat{y_i} = \sum_{i = 1}^n = e_i
\]
However, we assume that our errors are normally distributed with a mean of zero, so if we sum the residuals, we would add the positive and negative values together and they would be equal to zero.
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n  y_i - \hat{y_i} = \sum_{i = 1}^n  e_i = 0
\]
Instead, we can square our residuals and sum the squared residuals.
This is similar to estimating the variance of a random variable where we sum the squared deviations of the variable from its mean and then divide by \(N\).
\[
var(X) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i - \mu_x)^2
\]
Our objective function is the minimization of the sum of the squared residuals:
\[
\sum_{i = 1}^n (y_i - \hat{y})^2  = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2
\]
The question is: how do we arrive that estimates of the population parameters that minimize the sum of the squared residuals?

title: 9  Deriving Least Squares
text:
9.4 Objective Function
Let \(\boldsymbol{b_0}\) be a coefficient vector consisting of sample estimates of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) from a least squares regression.
The population regression function is:
\[\boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{X\beta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}\]
The sample regression function is:
\[\boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{X\ b_0} + \boldsymbol{e}\]
where the predicted values of the dependent variable are equal to:
\[
\boldsymbol{\hat{y}} = \boldsymbol{X \, b_o}
\]
and the residuals are equal to:
\[
\boldsymbol{e} = \boldsymbol{y - \hat{y}} = \boldsymbol{y - X \, b_0}
\]
Our objective function is the minimization of the sum of the squared residuals, that is, we choose \(\boldsymbol{b_0}\) such that the predicted values of the dependent variable best “fit” the data.
The sum of the squared residuals when we select \(\boldsymbol{b_0}\) is equal to:
\[
\boldsymbol{e_0^T \, e_0}
\]
We can now specific the objective function as:
\[min_{b0}\ S(b_0) = \boldsymbol{e_0^T e_0} = (\boldsymbol{y - \hat{y}})^T\  (\boldsymbol{y - \hat{y}})\]
\[e_0^T e_0 = (\boldsymbol{y - X\ b_0})^T\  (\boldsymbol{y - X\ b_0})\]
\[e_0^T e_0 = \boldsymbol{y^Ty - b_0^T\ X^T y - y^T\ Xb_0 + b_0^T X^T X b_0}\] It is important to note that:
\[\boldsymbol{b_0^T X^T y} \sim (1 \times K) \times (K \times n) \times (n \times 1) \sim (1 \times 1)\] \[\boldsymbol{y^T X b_0} \sim (1 \times n) \times (n \times K) \times (K \times 1) \sim (1 \times 1)\]
\[(\boldsymbol{b_0^T\ X^T y})^T = \boldsymbol{y^T\ X\ b_0}\]
We can substitute for \(\boldsymbol{y^T\ X\ b_0}\) to obtain:
\[min_{b0}\ S(b_0) =e_0^T e_0 = \boldsymbol{y^Ty - 2b_0^T\ X^T\ y + b_0^T X^T X b_0}\]

title: 9  Deriving Least Squares
text:
9.5 First Derivative
There are two useful identities that will help us in the derivation of the least squares estimator.
First, for the vectors \(\boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}\), the partial derivative of \(\boldsymbol{a^T}\) times \(\boldsymbol{b}\) with respect to \(\boldsymbol{a}\) is equal to \(\boldsymbol{b}\).
\[\frac{\delta \boldsymbol{a^Tb}}{\delta \boldsymbol{a}} = \boldsymbol{b}\]
Second, if \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is symmetric, then the first derivative of \(\boldsymbol{b^T A b}\) with respect to \(\boldsymbol{b}\) is:
\[\frac{\delta \boldsymbol{b^T A b}}{\delta \boldsymbol{b}} = 2 \boldsymbol{Ab} = 2 \boldsymbol{b^TA}\]
We can now return to the task at hand. We need to take the first derivative of the objective function with respect to \(\boldsymbol{b_0}\) and set the first derivative equal to zero or:
\[\frac{\partial(\boldsymbol{e_0^T e_0 )}}{\partial\ \boldsymbol{b_0}} = 0\]
\[\frac{\partial(\boldsymbol{e_0^T e_0 )}}{\partial\ \boldsymbol{b_0}} =\frac{\partial(\boldsymbol{y^Ty - 2b_0^T\ X^T\ y + b_0^T X^T X b_0})}{\boldsymbol{b_0}} = 0\]
\[\frac{\partial(e_0^T e_0 )}{\partial\ b_0} =\frac{\partial \,y^Ty}{\partial{b_0}} +  \frac{\partial \, 2b_0^T\ X^T\ y}{\partial b_0} + \frac{\partial \, b_0^T X^T Xb_0}{\partial \, b_0} = 0\]
Breaking the first derivative into its component parts yields:
\[\frac{\partial \,y^Ty}{\partial{b_0}} = 0 \]
\[\frac{\partial\ (-2\ \boldsymbol{b_0^T X^T y)}}{\partial\ \boldsymbol{b_0}} = -2 \boldsymbol{X^T y}\] \[\frac{\partial\ (\boldsymbol{b_0^T X^T X b_0})}{\partial\ \boldsymbol{b_0}} = 2\ \boldsymbol{X^T X\ b_0}\]
The first derivative of the objective function is equal to: \[\frac{\partial S(\boldsymbol{b_0})}{\partial \boldsymbol{b_0}} = -2\ \boldsymbol{X^T\ y} + 2\ \boldsymbol{X^T X\ b_0} = 0\]
If a solution \(\boldsymbol{b}\) exists, then the normal equations are: \[\boldsymbol{X^T\ X\ b} = \boldsymbol{X^T\ y}\]

title: 9  Deriving Least Squares
text:
9.6 First Derivative
If the full column rank assumption holds, then \((\boldsymbol{X^T X})\) is square as it is \((K \times K)\) and \((\boldsymbol{X^T X})\) is also symmetric.
Furthermore, if the full column rank assumption holds, then \((\boldsymbol{X^T X})\) has an inverse and we can use the normal equations to obtain the least square estimates of the population parameters.
\[\boldsymbol{X^T\ X\ b} = \boldsymbol{X^T\ y}\] \[\boldsymbol{b} = (\boldsymbol{X^T\ X})^{-1}\ \boldsymbol{X^T\ y}\] - The second derivative of the objective function is equal to: \[\frac{\partial^2 S(\boldsymbol{b_0})}{\partial \boldsymbol{b_0 b_0^T}} = 2\ \boldsymbol{X^T X}\] - \(2\ \boldsymbol{X^T X}\) is only a positive definite matrix if the full column rank assumption holds.

The least squares solution, if the full column rank assumption holds, is unique and minimizes the sum of the squared residuals \(e^Te\).

text:
9.6 Least Squares Estimator
If the full column rank assumption holds, then \((\boldsymbol{X^T X})\) is square as it is \((K \times K)\) and \((\boldsymbol{X^T X})\) is also symmetric.
If the full column rank assumption holds, then \((\boldsymbol{X^T X})\) has an inverse and we can use the normal equations to obtain the least square estimates of the population parameters.
\[\boldsymbol{X^T\ X\ b} = \boldsymbol{X^T\ y}\]
Given that the inverse of \(\boldsymbol{(X^T X)}\) exists, we can now solve for the least squares estimator.
We define the least squares estimator as “beta hat” and use b to denote the least squares estimator.
\[\boldsymbol{b} = (\boldsymbol{X^T\ X})^{-1}\ \boldsymbol{X^T\ y}\]

title: 9  Deriving Least Squares
text:
9.7 Second Derivative
If the first derivative is equal to zero, it informs us that the objective function has arrived at a minimum (or maximum). The first derivative being zero only means we have arrived at a stationary point.
We need the second derivative to provide that we have found a minimum instead of a maximum or a saddle point.
Starting with the first derivative:
\[\frac{\partial S(\boldsymbol{b_0})}{\partial \boldsymbol{b_0}} = -2\ \boldsymbol{X^T\ y} + 2\ \boldsymbol{X^T X\ b_0} = 0\]
We take the derivative of the first derivative to obtain the second derivative : \[\frac{\partial^2 S(\boldsymbol{b_0})}{\partial \boldsymbol{b_0 b_0^T}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{b_0 }} (-2\ \boldsymbol{X^T\ y} + 2\ \boldsymbol{X^T X\ b_0}) \]
We know that:
\[\frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{b_0}} (-2 \boldsymbol{X^T\ y}) = 0\] \[\frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{b_0}} (-2 \boldsymbol{X^T X b_0}) = \boldsymbol{2 X^T X}\]
In other words, the second derivative is equal to:
\[\frac{\partial^2 S(\boldsymbol{b_0})}{\partial \boldsymbol{b_0 b_0^T}} = 2\ \boldsymbol{X^T X}\]
For a point to be a local minimum, the Hessian matrix (second derivative) must be Positive Definite.
We know that \(\boldsymbol{X^TX}\) is always symmetric
We know that, for any non-zero vector, the quadratic form is at least positive semi-definite.
\[
\boldsymbol{v^T (X^TX)} = \boldsymbol{(Xv)^T(Xv)} = \boldsymbol{||Xv||^2}
\]
We know that, if \(\boldsymbol{X}\) has full column rank, then \(\boldsymbol{||Xv||^2} > 0\), which means that the second derivative is positive definite.
Because the second derivative is positive definite, the objective function is strictly convex and the stationary point (b) is a unique global minimum.

Simply put, because of the assumptions of linearity, full rank, and zero conditional mean, the least squares estimator minimizes (globally) the sum of the squared residuals.

title: 9  Deriving Least Squares
text:
9.8 Orthogonality of X and e
We can use \(\boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{X\ b} + \boldsymbol{e}\) and the normal equations to obtain: \[\boldsymbol{X^T\ X\ b} = \boldsymbol{X^T\ y}\] \[\boldsymbol{X^T X\ b} = \boldsymbol{X^T\ (\boldsymbol{X\ b} + \boldsymbol{e})}\] \[\boldsymbol{X^T X\ b} = (\boldsymbol{X^T X}) \boldsymbol{b} + \boldsymbol{X^T e}\] \[\boldsymbol{X^T e} = 0\]
Note that \(\boldsymbol{X^T e} = 0\) means that \(\boldsymbol{x_k^T e} = 0\).
The covariance between each independent variable and the disturbances is equal to zero.
This only occurs if the assumption of the exogeneity of the regressors (zero conditional mean) holds.
This illustrates why the assumptions of linearity, full rank, and strict exogeneity of the regressors are necessary to obtain the least squares estimates.

title: 9  Deriving Least Squares
text:
9.9 Projection
Imagine you have a flashlight and you are standing in a room.
The floor represents all the possible values that can be created by your independent variables.
There is a balloon floating above the floor. Let the balloon represent the dependent variable, y. Note that unless your model is perfect, the balloon will never touch the floor.

In other words, even if we have all the independent variables, we cannot perfectly explain y.
If you shine a flashlight directly above the balloon, you get a shadow on the floor. The shadow presents the predicted value of y created by the independent variables or \(\boldsymbol{\hat{y}}\).
In other words, the predicted value of y on the floor is the projection of y on X.
The projection of y on X is the best linear approximation of y using the information in X.
What is the best projection of y on X? Think of the lines from the floor to the balloon. We have a line at a 10 degree angle, 25 degree angle, and so on until we have a line at a 90 degree angle from the floor to the balloon.

We want the linear that minimizes the distance from our predicted value of y to the actual value of y.
A straight line from the floor to the balloon minimizes the distance, in other words, a line at a 90 degree angle from the floor, that is, a perpendicular line from y onto the floor.
Why is the “perpendicular line” the same as “minimizing the sum of squares”?
Think of the distance between the balloon, \(\boldsymbol{y}\), and any point on the floor, \(\boldsymbol{\hat{y}}\).
By the Pythagorean Theorem, the shortest distance between a point and a plane is always the perpendicular line.
The length of that perpendicular line is the magnitude of our residuals, \(\boldsymbol{||e||}\).
Minimizing the squared length of the residuals is mathematically identical to finding the orthogonal projection.
We now need to define how we can make the projection happen and what is “left over.”

title: 9  Deriving Least Squares
text:
9.12 M and P
M is symmetric and idempotent.
P is symmetric and idempotent.
M and P are orthogonal.
The residual maker and the projection matrix are orthogonal. \[\boldsymbol{PM} = \boldsymbol{MP} = \boldsymbol{0}\]
\[\boldsymbol{PM} = (\boldsymbol{X (X^T X)^{-1} X^T})(\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{X (X^T X)^{-1} X^T})\] \[\boldsymbol{PM} = \boldsymbol{X (X^T X)^{-1} X^T} - \boldsymbol{X (X^T X)^{-1} X^T}\boldsymbol{X (X^T X)^{-1} X^T}\] \[\boldsymbol{PM} = \boldsymbol{X (X^T X)^{-1} X^T} - \boldsymbol{X (X^T X)^{-1} X^T} = \boldsymbol{0}\]
When \(\boldsymbol{y}\) is pre-multiplied by \(\boldsymbol{M}\), it produces a vector of the least squares residuals:
\[\boldsymbol{e} = \boldsymbol{M y}\]
When \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is pre-multiplied by \(\boldsymbol{M}\) the result is: \[\boldsymbol{MX} = (\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{X (X^T X)^{-1} X^T})X\] \[\boldsymbol{MX} = \boldsymbol{X} - \boldsymbol{X (X^T X)^{-1} (X^T X)} = \boldsymbol{(X - X)} = \boldsymbol{0}\]
The regression of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is a perfect fit and the residuals from this regression are equal to 0.

title: 9  Deriving Least Squares
text:
9.13 Decomposing Y
We have previously specified the linear regression model as:
\[
\boldsymbol{y = X \beta + \epsilon}
\]
We can now decompose y into two parts: explained variation and unexplained variation.
\[
\boldsymbol{y = \hat{y} + e = Xb + e}
\]
We can also show the two parts are orthogonal, that is, there is no information in one part that provides information about the other part.
Building on this discussion, we can decompose y:
\[
\boldsymbol{y = \hat{y} + e = Xb + e}
\]
\[\boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{Py} + \boldsymbol{My}\]
And we know that P and M are orthogonal to each other, so Py and My are orthogonal to each other as well, showing that we can decompose y into two orthogonal components.
Because \(\boldsymbol{\hat{y}}\) and \(\boldsymbol{e}\) are orthogonal, there is zero correlation between them, that is, the residuals contain no information about the predicted values of the dependent variable and, likewise, the predicted values of the dependent variable contain no information about the residuals.
In the next section, we will work in R to illustrate these and other points.
